title: Gas Welding, Brazing, Soldering and Gas Cutting as it applies to Tractor Mechanic

lessons.title: Oxy-acetylene equipment and safe set-up
lessons.html:
Where gas processes fit in tractor work

A tractor mechanic uses oxy-acetylene equipment to heat seized bolts and bearings, cut damaged brackets, braze cast-iron or thin parts, and repair implements in the farm workshop. Soldering is used for electrical connections and small radiator repairs. These processes are useful but dangerous if done carelessly.

The equipment

  • Oxygen cylinder: usually black with a white shoulder in South Africa; high pressure; right-hand threads.
  • Acetylene cylinder: usually maroon; contains acetylene dissolved in acetone; left-hand threads, often with notched nuts.
  • Regulators: reduce cylinder pressure to working pressure; each has a cylinder and a working gauge.
  • Flashback arrestors: fitted at the regulators and often at the torch to stop a flame travelling back into the hoses and cylinders.
  • Hoses: blue or black for oxygen, red for acetylene.
  • Torch with welding tips or cutting attachment.

Always confirm cylinder identity by the label, not only colour.

Safe set-up

  1. Chain cylinders upright to a trolley or wall.
  2. Crack the oxygen valve briefly to blow dust out, standing to the side. Never do this near flames.
  3. Fit regulators and flashback arrestors; never use oil or grease on oxygen fittings because oil and oxygen can ignite violently.
  4. Open cylinder valves slowly. Open the acetylene valve only a small amount so it can be closed quickly.
  5. Set working pressures as given in the equipment maker's chart for the tip size.
  6. Test all joints for leaks with leak-detection solution.
  7. Purge each hose separately before lighting.

Lighting and shutting down

Light the acetylene first with a spark lighter, never a match or lighter, then add oxygen to get the required flame. To shut down, close the torch valves in the order the equipment maker specifies, then close cylinder valves and bleed the hoses. If a flashback occurs, close both cylinder valves at once and do not use the equipment until it has been checked.

lessons.title: Welding, brazing, soldering and cutting techniques
lessons.html:
Flame types

FlameMixtureUse
NeutralBalanced oxygen and acetyleneMost welding of steel
CarburisingExcess acetylene, feather on inner coneSome hardfacing and specific alloys
OxidisingExcess oxygen, short hissing coneSome brazing; harmful to steel welds

Gas welding

Fusion welding melts the edges of both parts and usually adds a filler rod. Clean the joint of rust, paint and oil. Tack the parts in place, then move the flame steadily so the molten pool forms evenly. Gas welding is slower than arc welding and is now used mostly for thin sheet and repairs where an arc welder is not suitable.

Brazing

Brazing joins metal without melting the parent metal. A bronze or brass filler melts and flows into the heated joint using flux. It is useful for cast iron, dissimilar metals and thin parts that would distort with welding. Heat the parts evenly to the temperature where the flux becomes clear and fluid, then apply the rod. A brazed joint is not as strong as a sound weld, so do not braze high-stress parts such as drawbars or hitch components.

Soldering

Soft soldering uses a low-melting tin-based solder with a soldering iron or small flame. Use it for electrical wire joins and copper or brass radiator repairs. For wiring, twist or crimp first, solder so the joint is bright and smooth, then insulate with heat-shrink. Use rosin flux for electrics; acid flux corrodes wires.

Oxy-fuel cutting

The cutting torch heats steel to a bright red, then a jet of pure oxygen burns through it. It works on mild and low-alloy steel, not on stainless steel, aluminium or cast iron. Keep the tip clean, hold a steady distance and speed, and support the piece so the off-cut falls safely.

Hazards and controls

  • Wear welding goggles with the correct shade, leather gloves, apron and boots.
  • Remove flammables; never cut or heat near fuel tanks, diesel lines or batteries.
  • Never cut or weld on a drum or tank that held fuel or chemicals unless it has been properly made safe.
  • Galvanised parts give off toxic zinc fumes; ventilate and avoid breathing fumes.
  • Keep a fire extinguisher nearby and watch for smouldering after work, especially near dry grass or chaff.
  • Under the OHS Act 85 of 1993, follow the workshop's hot-work rules.

Key points

  • Chain cylinders upright and fit flashback arrestors.
  • Never use oil or grease on oxygen fittings.
  • A neutral flame suits most steel welding.
  • Brazing does not melt the parent metal and is not for high-stress parts.
  • Oxy-fuel cutting works on mild steel, not stainless, aluminium or cast iron.
